scenes.visual: Title card: Coevolution Changes Both Partners. Show two interacting populations with arrows in both directions labelled selection, then evolutionary response. Carry these symbols into the opening scene.

scenes.tts: Coevolution means reciprocal evolutionary change. One species evolves in response to another. That change alters selection on its partner, which evolves in response. Why does this matter? A flower and a moth may fit each other even if only one evolved. A good fit alone cannot tell us whether both partners changed. We need evidence of change in both. That is how we distinguish coevolution from adaptation in just one partner.

scenes.visual: Animate a change in a flower trait, altered selection on a moth, then an evolutionary response in the moth. Label the arrows as changes across generations. Contrast this history with a static matching flower and moth carrying a question mark. End on the evidence requirement: reciprocal evolutionary change.

scenes.tts: First, measure what each partner gains or loses. Fitness means survival and reproduction. In mutualism, both gain. In parasitism, the parasite gains and the host loses. These are net outcomes. A root fungus takes carbon and supplies nutrients. It can help a plant in poor soil and cost it in rich soil. The outcome depends on conditions.

scenes.visual: Show paired fitness balances labelled Mutualism (+,+) and Parasitism (+,−). Then show a root fungus exchanging soil nutrients for plant carbon. Change the soil from poor to rich; show the plant balance shifting from net benefit to net cost. Keep both partner balances visible; identify the soil example as the plant-side outcome.

scenes.tts: How can mutualisms persist? Partner choice and host sanctions can help. Sanctions reduce the fitness of partners that stop providing a service. Rhizobia supply nitrogen to legumes in exchange for carbon. In soybean, researchers kept the bacterial strain the same but blocked nitrogen fixation with argon. The bacteria reproduced less in those nodules. Changing the service revealed a host sanction.

scenes.visual: Introduce partner choice and host sanctions as mechanisms that help mutualisms persist. Focus on soybean nodules: the same bacterial strain in air and in argon replacing nitrogen. Stop the nitrogen-service arrow in the argon condition, then show lower bacterial reproduction there. Label this result Soybean host sanction. Do not depict a conscious plant decision or assert an oxygen mechanism.

scenes.tts: For hosts and parasites, reciprocal change can take different forms. In an arms race, host resistance and parasite infectivity rise through repeated rounds. Escalation can slow or stop. In fluctuating selection, common host types are attacked most. Rare types gain, then the advantage shifts again. The contrast is escalation versus a changing advantage.

scenes.visual: Two schematic panels: Arms race shows resistance and infectivity rising through successive generations, with room for a plateau. Fluctuating selection shows host types changing in frequency as common types are attacked and rarer types gain. Use no numerical data or invented measured values.

scenes.tts: A time shift assay compares hosts with parasites from the past, present and future. An arms race predicts parasites infect past hosts best and future hosts worst. Fluctuating selection predicts a peak or dip on contemporary hosts, with no steady trend.

scenes.visual: Show a conceptual grid of host and parasite sampling times. Highlight past, contemporary and future pairings. Compare a directional infection trend with a contemporary peak or dip without a long-run trend. Label these Predictions, not measured results. Use relative axes without numerical values.

scenes.tts: Rapid evolution can also change population cycles. In rotifers and algae, grazing favours defended algae, but defence costs nutrient competitiveness. As rotifers decline, undefended clones regain ground. Changing algal clonal diversity changed the cycles. The manipulation and measured trade-off supported prey evolution driving population dynamics. Cycle timing alone was no proof. Predator evolution was not investigated, so this was not demonstrated coevolution.

scenes.visual: Closing application: rapid evolution feeds back on population dynamics. Show rotifer grazing favouring defended algal clones, label their poorer nutrient competitiveness, then show rotifers declining and undefended clones regaining ground. Follow the mechanism with a one-clone versus several-clone manipulation leading to different population cycles. Use qualitative curves with no specific lags, periods, peak times or arithmetic. End with Prey evolution shown; predator evolution not investigated, tied back to the opening two-way evidence requirement.
End card: Coevolution requires reciprocal evolutionary change. Reuse the opening two-way selection and evolutionary-response diagram. No phase-lag formula or numerical cycle comparison.
